Energy, Heat and Enthalpy: Thermochemistry studies the heat exchanged in chemical reactions. The system is the reaction and the surroundings are everything else. An exothermic reaction releases heat (the surroundings warm up) and has delta H negative; an endothermic reaction absorbs heat (the surroundings cool) and has delta H positive. Enthalpy change delta H is the heat at constant pressure and is measured in kJ or kJ/mol. A thermochemical equation includes delta H, for example CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O, delta H = -890 kJ. Reversing a reaction changes the sign of delta H, and multiplying the equation multiplies delta H. Energy diagrams show the activation energy and the energy of reactants and products.
Calorimetry and Specific Heat: A calorimeter measures heat. The heat absorbed or released by a substance is q = m c delta T, where c is the specific heat capacity (water 4.18 J/(g C)). In a coffee-cup calorimeter at constant pressure, the heat of the reaction is the opposite of the heat gained by the solution: q_rxn = -m c delta T. The enthalpy per mole is delta H = q_rxn / n. A bomb calorimeter measures the heat of combustion at constant volume using the heat capacity of the calorimeter. Heat lost by a hot object equals heat gained by a cold one when they are mixed.
Hess's Law and Standard Enthalpies of Fo: Hess's law says that the total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or in several steps, because enthalpy is a state function. To use it, add the steps (reverse equations change the sign, scaled ones scale delta H) so the target equation is obtained, and add their delta H values. The standard enthalpy of formation delta H_f is the heat of forming one mole of a compound from its elements in their standard states; for an element in its standard state it is zero. For any reaction: delta H_rxn = sum(n delta H_f of products) - sum(n delta H_f of reactants).
Bond Energies and Energy Changes: Chemical reactions involve breaking bonds, which absorbs energy, and forming bonds, which releases energy. The enthalpy change can be estimated from average bond energies: delta H = sum(bonds broken) - sum(bonds formed). If more energy is released in forming bonds than is needed to break bonds, the reaction is exothermic. Typical bond energies (kJ/mol): H-H 436, O=O 498, O-H 463, C-H 413, C=O 799, Cl-Cl 243, H-Cl 431. Bond energies give only estimates because they are averages and apply to gases. A higher bond energy means a stronger bond.
Entropy, Gibbs Free Energy and Spontanei: A spontaneous process occurs without continuous outside help. Entropy S measures the disorder or the number of ways energy can be distributed; it increases when a solid melts, a liquid vaporizes, a gas expands or the number of gas moles rises. The second law says that the total entropy of the universe increases in a spontaneous process. The Gibbs free energy combines enthalpy and entropy: delta G = delta H - T delta S, with T in kelvins. A reaction is spontaneous when delta G is negative, at equilibrium when delta G = 0 and non-spontaneous when delta G is positive. If delta H is negative and delta S positive, the reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures. Spontaneous does not mean fast.
